sweep_summary: Norwegian (norw1258) is in the catalog as weight-hedged (QS-HEDGED, right-edge three-syllable window; deciding source Rice 2006 / ROA-747). I re-fetched sources ROA-747 and verified the catalog quote at pp.1-2 and p.7. All five title-sweep items are about tonal accent (Accent 1/2) or Old Norwegian syntax, none about stress placement: Tiemann 2022 (Old Norwegian OV/VO, constituent weight; abstract read via Crossref, irrelevant); Withgott & Halvorsen 1988 (paywalled de Gruyter / restricted archive.org lending copy; tonal accent representation, low priority); Kelly & Smiljanić 2017 (Karger paywalled; abstract read, Trøndersk tonal accent acoustics, silent on stress); Wetterlin 2010 (paywalled, but its open 2006 Konstanz thesis was fetched sources and read — it presupposes stress and explicitly declines to state Standard East Norwegian stress rules); Morén 2005 (abstract recovered from the Wayback copy of the 13mfm booklet, scanned of an image page — boundary-tone analysis of stød/pitch accent, silent on stress placement). The best first-hand stress statement read is Lunden 2006 (ROA-833, on file from the earlier pass): final stress on consonant-final words, else penult, else antepenult when penult light and antepenult heavy, with listed minor patterns — confirms and refines the catalog coding without superseding Rice 2006. Still unread and worth acquiring for completeness (not for the coding): Kristoffersen 2000 The Phonology of Norwegian chs. 6-7 (OUP, paywalled) and Lunden 2013 JCGL (paywalled), both already noted in. all lookups were done by direct fetches (ROA, KOPS, Crossref, Europe PMC, Karger, Wayback/CDX).

new_statements.quote: I claim that stress falls on the final syllable when possible. The final syllable may bear stress if it is underlyingly /CVC/ or /CVCC/. (In the former instance it will be augmented to CV:C.) Stress is otherwise penultimate, a light /CV/ being augmented to CV:. The quantity sensitive nature of the language can be seen in words that have the shape /CVC.CV.CV/. In such cases the antepenult, rather than the penult, will be stressed, as it is underlyingly heavy. Thus, we may state the basic stress pattern as in (28). (28) a. If the word ends in a consonant, stress the final syllable b. Otherwise, stress the penult c. Unless the penult is light and the antepenult is heavy, in which case, stress the antepenult

new_statements.reading: A first-hand, lexicon-based (Kristoffersen's loanword database, checked with a native speaker) plus novel-word-experiment statement of Norwegian primary-stress placement: right-edge, quantity-sensitive three-syllable window — final stress on consonant-final (closed) finals, otherwise penult, antepenult only when the penult is light and the antepenult heavy; native words (mono- or CVX.C-disyllabic) have invariant initial stress; predictable minor patterns ([s]-, [Cs]-, [er]/[et]-final words take penult; final-hiatus V-final words take antepenult) and a residue of true exceptions (French/Greek vowel-final loans with final stress, bison). Lunden adds (p.108) that the pattern 'is thought to be consistent across dialects of Norwegian'. This CONFIRMS and REFINES the catalog's weight-hedged / QS-HEDGED coding built on Rice 2006 (right-edge alignment, NonFinality overridden by bimoraic finals, weight partly lexical): same window, same weight logic, with the exception classes spelled out. It does not contradict anything in the Rice quote.

sources.citation: Morén, Bruce (2005). Danish stød and Eastern Norwegian pitch accent: The myth of lexical tones. Paper presented at the 13th Manchester Phonology Meeting, 26-28 May 2005 (abstract in the 13mfm abstracts booklet).
sources.quote: The basic claim advanced in this talk is simple: Danish and E. Norwegian tones are completely predictable from prosodic and morphological context. Forms that are described as having 'stød' or 'Accent 1' have a low tone aligned to the right edge of a morphological (Danish) or prosodic (E. Norwegian) domain that is realized on the head syllable of a foot. ... Accent 1 invariably has a low trough toward the end of the stressed syllable, and Accent 2 invariably has a low trough toward the beginning of the post-stressed syllable.
sources.locator: 13mfm abstracts booklet, pdf p.14 (one-page abstract; only the abstract exists in print)
sources.note: An argument that Danish stød and East Norwegian Accent 1/2 are boundary-tone effects of foot structure rather than lexical tone; presupposes a stressed (foot-head) syllable but says nothing about where in the word stress falls. Silent on the catalog coding; nothing to acquire.

sources.quote: Two experiments examined the acoustic correlates of the disyllabic tonal accent contrast in the Trøndersk dialect of Norwegian, and how narrow focus and phrasal position shape the contrast. Production results showed that both tonal accents have a high-low (HL) pitch contour, with different timing. ... When at the right edge of an accent phrase (AP), the accents were shown to have a higher L, lower AP H% tone, shorter stressed vowel, and longer final vowel.
sources.note: Acoustic study of the Accent 1/Accent 2 tonal contrast (Trøndersk) under focus and phrase position; the abstract mentions a 'stressed vowel' only as the locus of the tonal contrast and says nothing about where stress is placed. Silent on the catalog coding.

sources.quote: Main stress is indicated with a straight apostrophe before the stressed syllable. For example, 'aksel1 'shoulder' has stress on the first syllable and Accent 1, whereas pa'rade2 'parade' has stress on the penultimate syllable and Accent 2. ... Although this divergent stress patterns would have to be accounted for in the rules of Standard East Norwegian stress, we will put that aside here since our analysis is concentrating on lexical accent assignment. ... more investigation ... would require a solid conception of how stress assignment works in Standard East Norwegian ... which is unfortunately not possible within the framework of this thesis.
sources.note: The thesis (and, by its title and de Gruyter TOC, the 2010 book) is about the lexical specification of tonal Accent 1/2 in Standard East Norwegian; it takes primary stress as given (examples marked 'aksel1, pa'rade2, pi'lot1, 'asosi,al), states that Accent 2 requires a disyllabic trochee bearing main stress so words with final stress and monosyllables are Accent 1, and explicitly declines to state the stress-assignment rules of Standard East Norwegian (pp. 135-136). No placement rule; silent on the weight-hedged coding. Book itself not needed.
